items.title: How to Build a Brand Identity From Scratch
items.desc: How to build a brand identity from scratch: name, logo, colors, and tone of voice, using free tools and no designer.
items.keys: Branding Start With a Name and a Feeling Design a Simple Logo Build Your Visual Identity Define Your Tone of Voice The Most Important Thing
items.text: When I started Velora Gran Turismo, I had no branding experience. I just knew I wanted it to look real, not like some kid's hobby project. So I figured it out. Here's what actually mattered. Start With a Name and a Feeling Your brand name should be easy to say, easy to remember, and give people a feeling. Velora Gran Turismo evoked speed, style, and automotive culture before anyone saw a single product. That's the goal. Ask yourself: what do I want people to feel when they see my brand? Write down three words. Those three words should guide every design decision you make. Design a Simple Logo You don't need to hire a designer. Use Canva or Adobe Express. Start with a wordmark (just your brand name in a distinctive font). Most strong brands start simple. Pick one or two fonts maximum. Pick a color palette of two to three colors. That's it. Consistency beats complexity every time. "A brand is not a logo. A brand is what people feel when they interact with you." Build Your Visual Identity Once you have a logo and colors, apply them everywhere consistently. Your Instagram profile, your website, your packaging, your email signature. The more consistent you are, the more real your business looks. Define Your Tone of Voice How does your brand talk? Formal or casual? Serious or playful? Write a few sample captions in your brand voice and stick to it. People should be able to read your posts and know it's you. The Most Important Thing Start. Don't spend three weeks perfecting your logo before you've sold anything. Launch with something good enough, learn from real customers, and improve as you go.

items.title: How to Set Up an Online Store for Free
items.desc: How to set up an online store for free or close to it: choosing a platform, print-on-demand with Printful, and a custom domain.
items.keys: E-Commerce Choose Your Platform Set Up Print-on-Demand If You're Selling Physical Products Get a Custom Domain Keep It Simple
items.text: When I built the Velora Gran Turismo store, I was 15 and had almost no budget. Here's exactly how I did it, and what I'd do differently today. Choose Your Platform For a product-based business, Shopify is the most complete option. It handles your store, payments, inventory, and shipping in one place. The basic plan costs money, but it's worth it once you're generating revenue. If you want to start completely free, try Big Cartel for small product ranges or WooCommerce if you already have a WordPress site. Set Up Print-on-Demand If You're Selling Physical Products This is what changed everything for me. With Printful, you design the product, list it on your store, and when someone orders, Printful prints and ships it directly to them. You never hold inventory. The margins are lower than buying wholesale, but the risk is zero. For a first business, that matters. Get a Custom Domain A custom domain costs around $12 a year on Namecheap. It makes your store look 10x more professional than a free subdomain. This is the one thing worth paying for immediately. Keep It Simple Three to five products maximum when you launch. A clean homepage, a product page, and a contact page. That's all you need. You can add complexity later once you understand what your customers actually want. "Your first store doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to exist."

items.title: Getting Started: What to Do When You Have an Idea But Don't Know Where to Begin
items.desc: Have an idea but don't know where to begin? How to validate it, start small, and land your first paying customer without overcomplicating it.
items.keys: Getting Started Validate Before You Build Start Smaller Than You Think Work Out What It Will Cost Price It Properly From Day One Pick One Thing and Do It Set a Deadline Get Your First Ten Customers The Only Thing That Matters at the Start
items.text: Having an idea is the easy part. Knowing what to do first is where most people get stuck. These are the steps that matter most at the very beginning. Validate Before You Build Before spending any money or time building, ask yourself one honest question: would anyone actually pay for this? Not would they say it's cool. Would they pay for it. Tell ten people about your idea and ask if they'd buy it. Not if they like it. If they'd buy it. The answer will tell you more than months of planning. Even better, ask for real commitment: Pre-sell it. Show a mock-up or sample and take orders before you produce anything. Name a price. "Would you buy this for $35?" gets a far more honest answer than "Do you like it?" Watch what people do, not what they say. Messages, orders and sign-ups count. Compliments don't. Start Smaller Than You Think Whatever you're planning, do a smaller version first. Want to sell clothing? Sell one product before building a full collection. Want to offer a service? Get one paying client before building a website. The first version isn't supposed to be perfect. It's supposed to teach you what your customers actually want. Work Out What It Will Cost Most first products can launch for much less than people expect, especially with print-on-demand, a free store plan and photos taken on your phone. But "probably not much" isn't a plan. Write down every cost before you spend anything: setup, first stock, monthly tools and a buffer for surprises. The free Startup Cost Estimator adds it all up for you, and shows how many sales it takes to earn the money back. Price It Properly From Day One Underpricing is the easiest way to work hard and make nothing. Know your true cost per item, then price for a healthy margin, not just "a bit more than it costs". The pricing guide explains how, and the Pricing Calculator does the maths. Pick One Thing and Do It The biggest mistake new entrepreneurs make is trying to do everything at once. One product. One platform. One marketing channel. Get that right before adding anything else. Set a Deadline Ideas without deadlines stay ideas. Give yourself a specific date by which you will have something live, even if it's rough. A deadline does more than motivation ever will. A simple 30-day plan looks like this: Week 1: validate. Talk to ten potential customers and name a price. Week 2: make a sample or a first version, and work out your costs. Week 3: set up a simple store or order form, and take good photos. Week 4: launch to the people who said yes, and ask them to share it. Get Your First Ten Customers Your first customers won't come from ads. They'll come from people who already know you, and from the people they tell. Start with the ten people you spoke to in week one, then friends, family, classmates and online communities where your customers already spend time. Treat every early customer like gold. Ask what they liked, what they'd change, and whether you can share their feedback. Those first reviews make it much easier to win customer number eleven. The Only Thing That Matters at the Start Revenue. Not followers, not a perfect logo, not a beautifully designed website. Your first goal is to get one person to hand you money for something. Everything else comes after that. "Done is better than perfect. Shipped is better than planned."

items.title: Getting Your First Customers Without a Budget
items.desc: How to get your first customers with zero budget, using TikTok, Instagram, direct outreach, and online communities.
items.keys: Marketing TikTok Is the Most Powerful Free Tool Available Right Now Build an Instagram Presence Use Direct Outreach Join Communities Where Your Audience Hangs Out
items.text: Nobody is going to find your store on their own. You have to bring them there. Here's how to do that with zero marketing budget. TikTok Is the Most Powerful Free Tool Available Right Now When I posted TikToks for Velora Gran Turismo, some of them hit over 1,000 views with no followers and no paid promotion. That's organic reach you simply cannot get on any other platform right now. You don't need to be a video expert. Film your process: designing a product, packing an order, showing the brand behind the scenes. Authenticity works better than production quality. Build an Instagram Presence Instagram is where people go to check if a brand is real. A clean, consistent feed with good product photos builds trust. Post consistently, use relevant hashtags, and engage with accounts in your niche daily. Use Direct Outreach Message people who might care about your product. Not spam. Real messages to real people who fit your audience. Personalized outreach converts far better than random social media posts. Join Communities Where Your Audience Hangs Out Reddit, Discord, Facebook Groups: find where your potential customers actually spend time. Contribute value, answer questions, build relationships. Only pitch when it's genuinely relevant. "The best marketing is when someone else tells people about your business."

items.title: Mistakes I Made: What Went Wrong With My First Business and What I'd Do Differently
items.desc: What went wrong with my first business, Velora Gran Turismo, and the lessons I'd apply if I started again today.
items.keys: Lessons I Spent Too Long on the Brand Before Selling Anything I Tried to Sell to Everyone I Didn't Track My Numbers Properly I Underestimated How Hard Marketing Is Closing It Was the Right Decision
items.text: I ran Velora Gran Turismo for seven months, and I made plenty of mistakes along the way. None of them sank the business, but each one cost me time or money. Here they are, so you don't have to repeat them. I Spent Too Long on the Brand Before Selling Anything I spent three months building the website and refining the brand before a single product went on sale. Looking back, I could have validated the whole idea in week one by selling one custom product to someone I knew. Instead I delayed revenue by months. Lesson: sell before you build. I Tried to Sell to Everyone Velora Gran Turismo was automotive-inspired clothing. But I marketed it like a general fashion brand instead of going deep into automotive communities where car enthusiasts actually spend their time. I spread myself too thin. Lesson: find your niche and go deep before going wide. I Didn't Track My Numbers Properly I knew roughly how much I was making but I wasn't tracking costs carefully enough. Platform fees, shipping, and production costs eat into your margins faster than you expect. By the time I understood my actual numbers, I had already underpriced some products. Lesson: set up a simple spreadsheet before your first sale. Know your numbers from day one. I Underestimated How Hard Marketing Is I assumed that if I built a good product, people would find it. They didn't. Marketing is a full-time job on top of everything else. I started too late and didn't invest enough time in it. Lesson: start building an audience before you launch. Sell to people who are already paying attention. Closing It Was the Right Decision In April 2025, I closed Velora Gran Turismo to focus on my IB studies. Building the business gave me practical experience, and I learned more than any class could have taught me. "Failure isn't about losing. It's about learning and moving forward."

items.title: How to Run a Small Business Day to Day
items.desc: The unglamorous side of running a small business: tracking your numbers, handling orders and shipping, customer service, and unit economics.
items.keys: Operations Track Everything From Day One Set Up a System for Orders and Shipping Customer Service Is Part of Marketing Understand Your Unit Economics
items.text: Operations isn't glamorous. It's invoicing, shipping, customer service, accounting. But it's what separates real businesses from hobbies. Track Everything From Day One Revenue, expenses, inventory, customer info: set up a spreadsheet before your first sale. I didn't do this early enough, and it cost me in lost profit margins. You don't need expensive software. A simple Google Sheet works perfectly fine when you're starting. Set Up a System for Orders and Shipping When an order comes in, you need to know exactly what to do. Who packs it? How long does it take? What's the shipping process? Write it down. Then automate as much as possible. Customer Service Is Part of Marketing Every customer interaction is a chance to turn someone into a repeat customer or a brand advocate. Respond quickly, solve problems, go above and beyond when it's reasonable. Understand Your Unit Economics Cost per unit + platform fees + shipping + returns = your true cost. Price above that with enough margin to cover marketing, mistakes, and growth. "Good systems let a small business run without you holding everything in your head."

items.title: Pricing: How to Price Your Product Without Underselling Yourself
items.desc: How to price your product without underselling yourself: know your costs, aim for a healthy margin, and test your prices.
items.keys: Pricing Start With Your Costs Understand Your Margin Margin Is Not Markup Price for Your Customer, Not Just Your Costs Don't Compete on Price Plan for Discounts Before You Give Them Test Your Pricing The Psychology of Pricing
items.text: When I launched Velora Gran Turismo, I underpriced some products because I didn't know my real costs yet. It's one of the most common mistakes new founders make, and one of the easiest to avoid. Start With Your Costs Before you set a price, know your costs. For a physical product that usually means: Production: what it costs to make or buy one item. Packaging: bags, boxes, labels, tissue paper. Shipping you pay: if you offer free shipping, it's your cost. Platform and payment fees: usually a percentage of the sale plus a small fixed fee per order. Add them all up. That's your floor. Your price has to be above this number or you're losing money on every single sale. Example Say you sell a printed hoodie. Production is $22, packaging is $1.50, you pay $5 for shipping, and your platform charges 3% plus $0.30 per order. Before the percentage fee, each hoodie costs you $28.80 . The 3% comes on top and grows with your price, so your real floor is a little higher: about $29.70 . Sell for less than that and every order loses money. Understand Your Margin Margin is the difference between what something costs you and what you sell it for, as a share of the price. If a product costs you $10 to make and you sell it for $20, your margin is 50%. Aim for at least 50% margin as a starting point. Lower than that and you have almost no room for marketing, mistakes, or the occasional discount. Example Back to the hoodie. Sell it for $60 and the 3% fee is $1.80. You keep $60 − $28.80 − $1.80 = $29.40 per sale , a margin of about 49%. That's healthy. Margin Is Not Markup This trips up a lot of first-time founders. Markup compares your profit to your cost. Margin compares your profit to your price. They are not the same number. Buy something for $10 and sell it for $20, and your markup is 100%, but your margin is only 50%. If you aim for "50% markup" thinking it means 50% margin, you'll end up with a margin of just 33%, and wonder where the money went. Price for Your Customer, Not Just Your Costs Your costs tell you the lowest price you can charge. They don't tell you the right price. That depends on who you're selling to and what else they could buy instead. Look at three or four similar products your customer would also consider. Where does yours fit? If your quality, design or story is better, you can charge more. Your costs are the floor; what customers are willing to pay is the ceiling. Aim somewhere between. Don't Compete on Price Lowering your price to undercut competitors is a race to the bottom. There will always be someone willing to go lower. Compete on quality, brand, and experience instead. Plan for Discounts Before You Give Them Discounts feel small to the customer and big to you, because they come straight out of your profit. Example Give 20% off the $60 hoodie and it sells for $48. The fee drops to $1.44, and you keep $48 − $28.80 − $1.44 = $17.76 . A 20% discount cut your profit by almost 40%. That's exactly why a healthy margin matters. It's what lets you run a launch offer without working for free. Test Your Pricing Your first price isn't your final price. Launch, see how people respond, and adjust. If everything sells out immediately you're probably priced too low. If nothing sells, price might be one of several things worth looking at. If you're unsure, start a little higher. Lowering a price later is easy, and customers like it. Raising one is much harder. The Psychology of Pricing A price just below a round number, like $19 instead of $20, feels noticeably cheaper than the one-dollar difference suggests. Round numbers do the opposite: they feel more premium. Pick the one that fits your brand. Small detail, but it makes a real difference. Want to run your own numbers? Use the free Rexyd Pricing Calculator to find your true cost, your break-even price, and a price with a healthy margin. "Pricing isn't about being cheap. It's about being fair to yourself and your customers."

items.title: Social Media Strategy: How to Build a Content Strategy From Zero
items.desc: How to build a social media content strategy from zero: pick one platform, post with purpose, stay consistent, and track what works.
items.keys: Social Media Pick One Platform First Understand What Works Where Post With a Purpose Consistency Beats Virality Engage, Don't Just Broadcast Track What Works
items.text: Most young founders start posting without a plan, then give up when nothing takes off. A simple strategy fixes that. Here's how to build one from zero followers. Pick One Platform First Don't try to be everywhere at once. Pick the platform where your audience spends the most time and focus on that until you have real traction. For most young entrepreneurs selling products, that's TikTok. Understand What Works Where TikTok rewards authenticity over polish. Behind the scenes content, process videos, and honest moments outperform ads every time. Instagram rewards consistency and aesthetics. A clean, on-brand feed builds trust before someone even reads a caption. LinkedIn rewards insight and credibility. Useful, opinionated posts about your industry get shared and build your reputation over time. Post With a Purpose Every post should do one of three things: educate, entertain, or inspire. If it doesn't fit one of those, it probably won't land. Consistency Beats Virality One viral post doesn't build a brand. Showing up consistently over months does. Post at least three times a week on your chosen platform and don't quit after two weeks because nothing happened yet. Engage, Don't Just Broadcast Reply to every comment. Comment on accounts in your niche. Social media is a conversation, not a billboard. The more you engage, the more the algorithm works in your favor. Track What Works Every platform has analytics. Check them weekly. Double down on what performs and cut what doesn't. Let data guide you, not just gut feeling. "Social media is not about followers. It's about building a community of people who care about what you're doing."

items.title: Pricing Calculator
items.desc: Free pricing calculator for young entrepreneurs. Enter your costs and fees to find your true cost per item, break-even price, and a price with a healthy margin.
items.keys: tool calculator price charge margin break-even cost fees currency
items.text: How It Works Your true cost is everything you pay for one sale: production, packaging, shipping and the platform's fixed fee. The percentage fee grows with your price, so the calculator includes it when working out what to charge. Price = (production + packaging + shipping + fixed fee) ÷ (1 − fee % − target margin %) The lowest price is your break-even point. Sell below it and you lose money on every order, even if sales look good. Pick the Right Number A price just below a round number, like 23.99 instead of 24, tends to feel like a better deal. A round number feels more premium. Choose the one that fits your brand, then test it with real customers and adjust. Check your platform's real fees before you set your price, since they vary by store builder and payment provider. For the full thinking behind this, read How to Price Your Product Without Underselling Yourself . Planning your launch budget too? The Startup Cost Estimator shows how much money you need to get started, and how many sales it takes to earn it back.

items.title: Startup Cost Estimator
items.desc: Free startup cost estimator for young entrepreneurs. Add up your setup costs, first stock and monthly costs to see how much money you need to launch.
items.keys: tool calculator launch budget startup costs stock buffer money needed
items.text: How It Works The estimate adds up three things: what you pay once to get set up, the stock you buy before your first sale, and the monthly costs you'll have before sales cover them. A buffer goes on top, because almost every launch costs more than planned. Total = (setup + stock + monthly costs × months) × (1 + buffer %) Keep It Low The cheapest launch is a small one. Print-on-demand removes the biggest upfront cost, a free store plan can cover your first months, and your phone takes good enough photos. Start with what you need to make your first sale, and spend more once customers prove the idea works. Already know your costs per item? Use the Pricing Calculator to set a price that covers them, then come back to see how many sales it takes to earn your launch money back. For the bigger picture, read Getting Started .

items.title: Discount Calculator
items.desc: Free discount calculator for young entrepreneurs. See how much profit a sale really costs you, how many extra orders you need to make up for it, and the deepest discount you can afford.
items.keys: tool calculator discount sale offer promo profit percent off black friday
items.text: How It Works A discount comes straight out of your profit, because your costs stay the same. Only the percentage fee gets a little smaller. Profit = price − (production + packaging + shipping + fixed fee) − price × fee % To earn the same total profit with a discount, you need full-price profit ÷ discounted profit times as many sales. That’s the “extra sales” number. Use Discounts on Purpose A launch offer or a seasonal sale can be worth it, as long as you know the cost. Pick a discount your margin can handle, set an end date, and check whether it actually brought in enough extra orders. For the full thinking behind this, read How to Price Your Product Without Underselling Yourself . Still setting your price? The Pricing Calculator finds a price with a healthy margin first.

items.title: About VenturePanda
items.desc: Meet Krish Panda, the student entrepreneur and youth advocate who founded Rexyd to demystify complex corporate and startup logistics for peers.
items.text: About Rexyd Rexyd was built out of a simple realization: when I started my first business, I had no idea where to begin. At 15, I founded Velora Gran Turismo , an automotive-inspired clothing brand I built and ran entirely on my own for 7 months. Along the way, I taught myself branding, e-commerce, digital marketing, web design, customer service, and the day-to-day realities of running a business. There was no single place that gave me practical, straightforward advice as a young entrepreneur. Rexyd is that place. This isn't generic business advice from someone who read it in a textbook. Everything here comes from firsthand experience, building something from scratch, making mistakes, solving problems, and learning as I went. Whether you have an idea and don't know where to start, or you're already building and need specific guidance, Rexyd is here to help you move forward. Written by Krish Panda : IB Student, Founder, and School Chapter Director at the International Economics Post.
